issues.description: The problem statement (UML and explicit note) requires the name getter and setter to have protected visibility, but the solution implements getName() and setName() as public. This is a visibility mismatch that contradicts the specified encapsulation in the exercise and may confuse students about the intended access level for these methods.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the Animal.getName() and Animal.setName(...) methods protected in the solution (change their visibility to protected) to match the UML and explicit instructions in the problem statement, or alternatively update the problem statement/UML to accept public accessors if a public API was intended.

issues.description: The UML in the problem statement indicates the Animal(String) constructor should be protected (UML shows '#'), but the solution defines the Animal constructor as public. This visibility inconsistency could confuse students about the intended construction/encapsulation semantics of the abstract Animal class.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the Animal(String) constructor in the solution to protected to align with the UML in the problem statement, or update the UML/problem text to indicate a public constructor if that was the intended design.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML explicitly require the Animal name getter and setter to have protected visibility (allowing subclass access while restricting external access). In the solution, Animal.getName() and Animal.setName(...) are implemented as public methods. This mismatches the visibility specified in the exercise instructions and UML, creating a semantic inconsistency about the intended accessibility of these methods.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the problem statement by changing the getter and setter visibility in Animal.java to protected (i.e., declare protected String getName() and protected void setName(String)). Alternatively, if public visibility is intended, update the problem statement/UML to allow public access to the name getter/setter.
